slides.heading: A giant goal
slides.text: In 1961, President John F. Kennedy asked America to land a person on the Moon and bring them home safely before the end of the 1960s.

slides.heading: The crew
slides.text: Three astronauts were chosen: Neil Armstrong, the commander; Buzz Aldrin, who would land with him; and Michael Collins, who would fly the spaceship around the Moon.

image.alt: The three Apollo 11 astronauts in spacesuits

slides.credit: Photo: NASA · Armstrong, Collins and Aldrin

slides.heading: Two spaceships in one
slides.text: Apollo 11 had two spaceships: Columbia, where the crew lived, and Eagle, the lander that would touch down on the Moon.

slides.heading: The biggest rocket
slides.text: They rode on a Saturn V rocket, 110.6 meters (363 feet) tall. That's taller than the Statue of Liberty!

slides.heading: Apollo 11 highlights
slides.text: Here is NASA's short film of the whole adventure, from liftoff to leaving the Moon. Now it's your turn to live it!

intro: To reach the Moon we need the right parts. The checklist on the left shows exactly what Apollo 11 needs.
Tap parts to add them to the rocket. You can pick any part you like, but the rocket will only fly with the right ones!
partsList.wrongIntro: Hold on! These parts would make the mission fail:
partsList.doneLine: Perfect! That's everything Apollo 11 needs. Let's see the whole rocket stacked together!

parts.name: Launch Escape Tower
parts.info: Could pull the crew to safety if something went wrong during launch.

parts.name: Jet Engine
parts.why: Jet engines need air to breathe. Rockets carry their own oxygen, so they work in space.

parts.name: Command Module 'Columbia'
parts.info: Where the three astronauts lived. The only part that came back to Earth.

parts.name: Stage 1 (S-IC)
parts.info: The biggest stage, with five huge F-1 engines to lift the rocket off the ground.

parts.name: Mercury Capsule
parts.why: It only fits one astronaut. Apollo 11 had a crew of three!

parts.name: Service Module
parts.info: Held the main engine, fuel, oxygen and power for the trip.

parts.name: Solar Panels
parts.why: Apollo made electricity with fuel cells, which also made drinking water. Solar panels would just add weight.

parts.name: Stage 2 (S-II)
parts.info: Five J-2 engines pushed Apollo 11 higher and faster, almost to orbit.

parts.name: Moon Buggy
parts.why: The Moon buggy first went to the Moon on Apollo 15, in 1971. Apollo 11's astronauts explored on foot.

parts.name: Lunar Module 'Eagle'
parts.info: The lander that carried two astronauts down to the Moon's surface.

parts.name: Shuttle Wings
parts.why: The Moon has no air, so wings can't help there. Wings came later, with the Space Shuttle.

parts.name: Stage 3 (S-IVB)
parts.info: One J-2 engine that fired twice: once to reach orbit, and again to head for the Moon.

parts.name: Redstone Rocket
parts.why: Much too weak. It lifted Freedom 7 to space, but the Moon is about 384,000 km away!

parts.name: Instrument Unit
parts.info: The rocket's brain: a ring of computers that steered the Saturn V.

saturnReveal.title: The Saturn V
saturnReveal.subtitle: The rocket that carried Apollo 11
saturnReveal.line: Here it is: the mighty Saturn V, with Apollo 11 on top! Drag to spin it. Next, let's discover how hard it was to build.

intro: About 400,000 people worked on Apollo! Let's find out how hard some of the parts were to make.
Tap each glowing dot on the rocket to read its story. Then choose how hard it was to build. I'll tell you straight away if you're right!
research.panelHint: Tap a glowing dot on the rocket to start.
research.chooseLabel: How hard was it to make?
research.doneLine: You found out how hard each part was to make. Every one needed brilliant ideas and a lot of hard work!

categories.name: Hard
categories.desc: Made an old idea much, much better

categories.name: Very hard
categories.desc: Needed new materials and careful handwork

categories.name: Extremely hard
categories.desc: Nothing like it had ever been built

items.name: F-1 Rocket Engines
facts: The F-1 is still the most powerful single-nozzle liquid-fuel rocket engine ever flown.
Early test engines shook themselves apart. Engineers even set off small bombs inside them until they found a design that stayed steady.
Rocket engines already existed. The F-1 made that idea much, much bigger.
items.explain: Rocket engines already existed, so the F-1 was an old idea made much bigger and better. (Still super hard!)

items.name: Lunar Module
facts: It was the first crewed spaceship built to fly only in space. It was never meant to fly through Earth's air.
To save weight, some of its walls were about as thin as a few sheets of paper.
It was test-flown on Apollo 9 and Apollo 10 before it landed on Apollo 11.
items.explain: Nobody had ever built a spaceship to land on another world before. It was brand new.

items.name: Apollo Guidance Computer
facts: It was one of the first computers to use tiny computer chips called integrated circuits.
Its programs were woven by hand: workers threaded copper wires through or around tiny magnetic rings to store the 1s and 0s.
Margaret Hamilton led the team that wrote its flight software. No computer like it had ever flown people to another world.
items.explain: A computer small enough to fly to the Moon had never existed. The team had to invent it.

items.name: Heat Shield
facts: Coming home, the capsule hit the air at almost 40,000 km/h. The shield faced about 2,760 °C (5,000 °F).
Workers filled a honeycomb of hundreds of thousands of tiny cells with a special material, one cell at a time, by hand.
It was made to slowly char and flake away, carrying the heat off with it.
items.explain: The heat shield needed a special new material and a huge amount of careful handwork.

items.name: Spacesuits
facts: Each Moon suit had about 21 layers to protect against heat, cold and tiny specks of space dust.
After a fire during a ground test in 1967, engineers created a new fireproof fabric called Beta cloth.
Skilled seamstresses sewed the suits by hand, with every stitch in exactly the right place.
items.explain: The suits needed new fireproof materials and very careful sewing by hand.

intro: Apollo 11 wasn't just three astronauts. Thousands of people on Earth had to talk to each other all the time!
Connect the teams the way messages really travelled. Drag a wire from one team to another, or tap one and then the other. Follow the clues on the right.
wiring.doneLine: Every team is connected! This network of people kept Apollo 11 safe from launch to splashdown.
wiring.genericWrong: These two teams didn't talk directly. Think about who passes the message along!

links.clue: Radio calls from the astronauts are caught by giant dish antennas on Earth.
The tracking stations pass the voices and data on to Mission Control.
Once the rocket clears the tower, Launch Control hands the flight to Mission Control.
When there's a problem, Mission Control asks engineers and scientists for help.
Mission Control keeps NASA Headquarters updated.
NASA Headquarters reports to the President and the government.
Mission Control tells the recovery ship where the capsule will splash down.
Mission Control sends the TV pictures on to the networks, so the whole world can watch.

wrong.why: Close! Radio calls from space are caught by the giant antennas first, then passed to Mission Control.
The President did call the astronauts on the Moon, but the call went through Mission Control and the antennas.
The TV pictures from the Moon went through the antennas and Mission Control first.
The crew talked to Launch Control before liftoff, but in this map we follow the flight after it leaves the pad.

intro: It's launch day: July 16, 1969! Before liftoff, the launch team goes through a long checklist.
Copy each arrow sequence to finish every step. Use the arrow keys, tap the arrow buttons, or swipe in the right direction.

steps.name: Access arm swings away
steps.fact: The walkway the astronauts used to climb aboard swings back from the rocket.

steps.name: Fuel tanks pressurized
steps.fact: Gas is pumped into the tanks to push the fuel toward the engines.

steps.name: Switch to internal power
steps.fact: About 50 seconds before liftoff, the rocket switches to its own batteries.

steps.name: Ignition sequence start
steps.fact: About 9 seconds before liftoff, the five F-1 engines start up.

steps.name: Release hold-down arms
steps.fact: Giant arms hold the rocket down until the engines reach full power. Then they let go!

launch.liftoffLine: Liftoff! We have liftoff of Apollo 11!

slides.heading: The real liftoff
slides.text: On July 16, 1969, at 9:32 in the morning, Apollo 11 lifted off from Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

image.alt: The Saturn V rocket lifting off with fire and smoke

slides.heading: NASA footage
slides.text: Watch NASA's footage of the mission, starting with the launch. The ground shook for miles as the five F-1 engines roared!

slides.heading: Next stop: the Moon
slides.text: After less than 3 hours circling Earth, the third stage fired again and sent Apollo 11 on its way to the Moon.

intro: Apollo 11 is on its way to the Moon! The trip takes about 3 days.
Move up and down to dodge satellites near Earth, and space rocks and dust further out. Use the arrow keys, or touch and drag.

facts.text: Near Earth, we pass satellites circling our planet.
The Moon is about 384,000 km (239,000 miles) away.
Tiny specks of space dust zoom by at incredible speeds!

dodge.resultText: Now Michael Collins stays in Columbia, circling the Moon, while Neil and Buzz fly Eagle down to the surface.

intro: This is it! Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin fly Eagle down to the Moon.
Hold THRUST to slow down, and use the side jets to move left and right. Land gently on the flat, safe spot with the green lights. Keep your speeds green!
Eagle's shadow shows where you will land. If it gets tricky, switch on Landing help and the computer will slow you down for you.
landing.controls: Keys: Up or Space = thrust · Left/Right = side jets · H = landing help
landing.helpOn: Landing help is on! The computer keeps you slow. You just steer to the green lights.
landing.helpOffer: The real Eagle had a computer to help, too! Want Landing help? It keeps your down speed gentle, so you only need to steer.

tips.hover: Not there yet! Hold THRUST to stay up

landing.alarm: Program alarm 1202! The computer has too much to do... Mission Control: 'We're GO on that alarm!'
landing.lowFuel: Mission Control: '30 seconds!' Not much fuel left!
landing.offPad: Bumpy ground here! Hold THRUST to hop up, then fly over to the green lights.
landing.successText: Just like the real landing on July 20, 1969! Neil Armstrong flew past a crater full of boulders to find a safe spot, with only seconds of fuel to spare.
landing.crashFast: Too fast! Hold THRUST as you get close to the ground.
landing.crashSide: Sliding sideways too fast! Stop drifting before you touch down.
landing.crashRocks: Those are boulders! Aim for the flat, safe spot.
landing.crashFuel: Out of fuel! Try using thrust in short bursts.

slides.heading: "The Eagle has landed."
slides.text: This NASA film was shot through Eagle's window as it came down. After touchdown, Neil Armstrong radioed: 'Houston, Tranquility Base here. The Eagle has landed.'

video.credit: Video: NASA · The Flight of Apollo 11 (1969 film)

slides.heading: One small step
slides.text: Armstrong stepped onto the Moon and said: 'That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.' Watch NASA's footage of the moonwalk!
slides.speak: Armstrong stepped onto the Moon and said: That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind. Watch NASA's footage of the moonwalk!

slides.heading: Planting the flag
slides.text: Buzz Aldrin joined Neil on the surface. Together they set up a flag and science experiments, and collected Moon rocks.

image.alt: Buzz Aldrin standing beside the flag on the Moon

slides.credit: Photo: NASA · Buzz Aldrin and the flag

intro: Scientists back on Earth were waiting to study real Moon rocks!
First, tap each item on the ground to collect it. Then we'll sort everything into the right boxes for the scientists.
samples.sortIntro: Great collecting! Now drag each item into the right box. Look closely at the rocks!
samples.doneLine: Apollo 11 brought back 21.5 kg (47.5 pounds) of Moon rocks and soil. The crew also left science behind: a seismometer to feel moonquakes, and a laser mirror that scientists still bounce lasers off today!

items.name: First soil sample
items.fact: Neil Armstrong scooped this up first, just in case they had to leave in a hurry.

items.name: Dark rock
items.fact: Basalt formed from lava. The tiny holes were gas bubbles!

items.name: Speckled rock
items.fact: Breccia is broken rock glued together when space rocks crashed into the Moon.

items.name: Solar wind foil
items.fact: This foil caught tiny particles from the Sun. It was rolled up and brought back to Earth!

items.name: Dark rock
items.fact: The dark 'seas' of the Moon are made of old lava rock like this.

items.name: Core tube
items.fact: Tubes hammered into the ground collected layers of Moon soil.

items.name: Speckled rock
items.fact: Breccias tell the story of billions of years of crashes on the Moon.

items.name: Camera film
items.fact: Film from the Moon cameras. It held the famous photos of the moonwalk!

items.name: Dark rock
items.fact: Some Apollo 11 basalts are about 3.6 to 3.9 billion years old.

items.name: Bag of Moon dust
items.fact: Moon dust is powdery and sticky. It clung to the astronauts' suits!

intro: Back inside Eagle, Buzz Aldrin spotted a problem: a switch had broken off! Without it, the engine that lifts them off the Moon might not start.
Drag the right tool onto the broken switch. Think carefully: there's electricity inside!

tools.name: Metal screwdriver
tools.why: Metal carries electricity. It could cause a spark inside the switch!

tools.name: Hammer
tools.why: Too rough! You could break the whole panel.

tools.name: Tape
tools.why: Tape can't push the switch in. It needs to be pressed firmly.

repair.fixedLine: It worked! Buzz Aldrin really used a felt-tip pen, because it wasn't made of metal. Eagle lifted off the Moon and met up with Columbia.
repair.separateIntro: Almost home! Before hitting Earth's air, the crew leaves the Service Module behind. Only the Command Module has a heat shield. Hold the button to separate!
repair.separatedLine: Separated! Now only Columbia, the Command Module, is heading home.
repair.aimIntro: The heat shield must face forward, into the air. Turn the capsule until the shield points at the arrow.
repair.aimDone: Shield forward! That's where the heat will hit.
repair.angleIntro: Now choose the entry angle. Too steep and it gets too hot. Too shallow and the capsule skips off the air like a stone on water! Slide into the green zone.
repair.tooSteep: Too steep! Too hot and too bumpy.
repair.tooShallow: Too shallow! It would skip off the air.
repair.doneLine: Columbia is lined up perfectly for re-entry. Here we go!

slides.heading: Re-entry!
slides.text: Columbia hit Earth's air at almost 40,000 km/h (25,000 mph). The air in front of it glowed, and the heat shield reached about 2,760 °C (5,000 °F), but the crew inside stayed safe.

slides.heading: NASA footage
slides.text: Here is NASA's 1969 film of Apollo 11 coming home: the recovery ship waiting at dawn, the glowing capsule streaking across the sky, and sailors watching for it.

video.credit: Video: NASA · The Flight of Apollo 11 (1969 film)

slides.heading: Blackout
slides.text: For a few minutes, the super-hot air around the capsule blocked the radio. Mission Control waited to hear the crew's voices again.

slides.heading: Parachutes next!
slides.text: Once the capsule slowed down, it was time for the parachutes. Get ready to help!

intro: Columbia is falling through the sky. You're in charge of the parachutes and the safety gear!
Press the button when the height meter reaches the green zone. First the small drogue parachutes, then the three big main parachutes.
splashdown.tooEarly: Too early! Wait for the green zone.
splashdown.auto: The automatic backup opened them for you. Try to be quicker next time!
splashdown.drogueOk: Drogue chutes open! They steady the capsule and slow it down.
splashdown.mainOk: Three big main parachutes! Now we float down gently.
splashdown.flipIntro: Splashdown in the Pacific Ocean! But the capsule landed upside down, just like the real Apollo 11. Tap the three balloon bags to flip it upright!
splashdown.flipDone: Upright! The balloon bags turned the capsule the right way up.
splashdown.gearIntro: Now switch on the safety gear so the rescue team can find us. Tap each one!

gear.name: Cut parachutes loose
gear.fact: So the wind can't drag the capsule across the waves.

gear.name: Flashing light
gear.fact: A bright flashing light helps rescuers see the capsule.

gear.name: Radio beacon
gear.fact: It beeps a radio signal that helicopters can follow.

gear.name: Green dye marker
gear.fact: Bright green dye spreads in the water, easy to spot from the air.

splashdown.doneLine: All safety gear is on. Now let's switch places and help the rescue team find the crew!

intro: You are flying the recovery helicopter, called Helicopter 66, from the ship USS Hornet.
Follow the radio beeps: the faster they beep, the closer you are. The arrow points toward the signal. Use the arrow keys, or touch where you want to fly.
rescue.found: Found them! Swimmers jump in to help.
steps: Swimmers attach a floating collar around the capsule.
The astronauts put on special suits in case they brought back Moon germs.
The helicopter lifts the crew up in a basket.
rescue.homeLine: Welcome home! The crew landed on the USS Hornet, where President Nixon was waiting to greet them. Then they spent about three weeks in quarantine, just in case.

pages.title: Mission report: Apollo 11

image.alt: Buzz Aldrin walking on the Moon near Eagle
image.credit: Photo: NASA · Buzz Aldrin on the Moon

pages.say: Apollo 11 launched on July 16, 1969, landed on the Moon on July 20, and splashed down safely on July 24. The whole mission took just over 8 days.

pages.title: The steps that led to the Moon

items.name: Explorer 1 & NASA
items.text: America's first satellite, and NASA begins.

items.name: Freedom 7
items.text: Alan Shepard, the first American in space.

items.name: Friendship 7
items.text: John Glenn, the first American to orbit Earth.

items.name: Gemini
items.text: Practice: spacewalks, meeting up and docking in space.

items.name: Apollo 8
items.text: The first people to fly around the Moon.

items.name: Apollo 11
items.text: The first people to walk on the Moon!

pages.say: Each mission taught NASA something new: from the first satellites, to flying people in space, to practicing spacewalks and docking, and finally flying around the Moon. Step by step, they got ready for Apollo 11.

pages.title: What Apollo gave the world

items.name: Computer chips
items.text: Apollo was one of the first big users of computer chips, helping them grow into the devices we use today.

items.name: Software engineering
items.text: Margaret Hamilton's team helped make writing software a real engineering job.

items.name: Cordless tools
items.text: Battery-powered drills made for Apollo helped inspire cordless tools.

items.name: Moon science
items.text: Moon rocks are still studied today, and scientists still bounce lasers off the mirror Apollo 11 left behind.

pages.say: Apollo's hard work still helps us today: better computer chips, careful software, cordless tools, and science that continues more than fifty years later.

complete.title: Mission accomplished!
lines: You built the Saturn V and learned how hard Apollo was to make.
You connected Mission Control and launched Apollo 11.
You landed Eagle on the Moon and collected samples.
You brought the crew home safely!
complete.guide: You did it, star sailor! From the very first satellite all the way to the Moon. More adventures are coming soon: Apollo 13, Voyager, Mars rovers and the James Webb Space Telescope!
